reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because its purpose is to answer skateboarding questions and provide instruction about tricks, equipment, and board setup. It shows Tony Hawk demonstrating skateboarding activity alongside a viewer question and instructional reply. The subscription request is ordinary channel engagement and is not linked to payment, investment, credential submission, or another deceptive participation flow.

citations.quote: My first advice to you is learn how to skate quarter pipes
I do know how to set up a skateboard.
You just need to snap the tail. And then slide your front foot simultaneously. To bring the tail up, that's an ollie.
Tony also demonstrates how to set up a new skateboard, how to apply griptape, how to do an ollie, how to boardslide, how to do a 540° McTwist and more.

opening.argument: Judge, consider the giveaway language alongside the requests for audience action. Hawk says he gives away skateboards to people, while the description directs viewers to a Skate Support account and asks them to subscribe. The video does not explicitly promise a board to anyone who follows or subscribes, but that gap is precisely why the solicitation deserves scrutiny: viewers hear about accessible giveaways and are then given channels through which to engage.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The instructional passages are real, but they do not resolve the concern about the separate giveaway and engagement language. Explaining board setup or an ollie does not tell the judge what a viewer might expect after hearing that skateboards are given away and being directed to an account. Nor does the absence of a payment request alone settle whether the invitation is misleading.

citations.quote: I give away my skateboard so much for auctions,. For charities, and for people.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The giveaway remark describes Hawk's own practice, including auctions and charities; it offers viewers no board and sets no condition for receiving one. The account link is identified as Skate Support, and the subscription request names WIRED. None of the cited text connects either action to a reward. The demonstrated instruction is the substance of the video, not a claim flow.

opening.argument: Judge, the cautionary signals here are modest but should be read together. A recognizable skateboarder speaks about giving boards away; the description supplies an external social account and asks for a subscription. His authority and the hands-on demonstration could make those invitations feel especially credible. There is no stated fee or urgent deadline, but neither is there an explanation that rules out viewers interpreting the giveaway remark as a reason to make contact.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense identifies genuine instruction, but instructional credibility can also strengthen an audience invitation. Its cited trick and setup explanations do not address why the description includes an external account or how a viewer should understand the remark about giving boards away. Those points warrant consideration even though the video states no payment demand.

citations.quote: I give away my skateboard so much for auctions,. For charities, and for people.
Tony's Skate Support Twitter Account https://twitter.com/skatesupport_TH

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These signals do not add up to a deceptive offer. Hawk says he gives boards away in the course of describing why he is accustomed to new skateboards, not while asking viewers to claim one. The external account is presented as Skate Support; the subscription request is ordinary channel engagement. No cited passage promises a reward for either action.

citations.quote: I had to learn how to break in new skateboards constantly. And now that's more what I'm used to.
Tony's Skate Support Twitter Account https://twitter.com/skatesupport_TH
Still haven't subscribed to WIRED on YouTube?

opening.argument: Judge, this is more than an isolated lesson: the description also directs viewers to a named social account, asks them to subscribe, and promotes where to find more WIRED shows. The skateboarding answers provide a credible setting for those invitations. In that setting, Hawk's statement that he gives boards away to people can serve as an additional reason for a viewer to stay engaged. The question is whether the educational presentation obscures the promotional effect of the whole package.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense is right that the video teaches tricks and board setup. That does not make the surrounding promotion disappear: the description directs viewers to an account and asks for a subscription. Its claim that no payment or credential request appears addresses one risk, but it does not by itself explain the effect of placing giveaway language inside a presentation that also seeks audience engagement.

citations.quote: Tony's Skate Support Twitter Account https://twitter.com/skatesupport_TH
Still haven't subscribed to WIRED on YouTube?
I give away my skateboard so much for auctions,. For charities, and for people.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Promotion of a channel or related account is not itself a reward solicitation. The description identifies the video as answers to skateboarding questions, and Hawk gives concrete setup and trick instruction. His giveaway comment explains why he regularly breaks in new boards; it does not invite viewers to follow, subscribe, or contact anyone to obtain one. The proposed connection between those passages is unsupported.
